name: Social Security
description: Iran’s social security arrangements combine employment-related insurance with separate welfare and assistance programmes. Understanding the distinction helps explain why receiving a cash subsidy does not establish entitlement to a retirement pension or other insured benefits.

seo.title: Social Security in Iran: Insurance, Institutions and Coverage
seo.description: Understand Iran’s employment-related social insurance, its principal institutions, and the distinction between insured benefits and social assistance.

content.heading: Insurance against interrupted income
content.content:
Social security in Iran is broader than retirement. The Social Security Law catalogued by the International Labour Organization was adopted in 1975. Its translated text covers accident and sickness protection, maternity, disability, retirement and death-related benefits, alongside provisions for marriage grants and family allowances. These categories describe a legal framework; they do not establish that every resident receives every benefit. [s1][s2]

The law links protection to insured status. Its provisions address wage and salary workers, while an amendment reproduced in the translation provides for self-employed people to obtain all or some insured benefits under implementing regulations. This distinction matters: a person’s occupation, contribution arrangement and insured benefit package must be understood before describing their protection. The archived translation is useful for explaining the system’s foundations, but it is not a consolidated statement of every rule applicable at the research cutoff. [s2]

content.heading: Several institutions, different routes into protection
content.content:
The Social Security Organization, often abbreviated SSO, is a principal provider of insurance associated with employment. A research chapter published by the Canadian government distinguishes its coverage from that of the Civil Service Pension Fund, which serves government employees, and from separate arrangements for military and security personnel. It also distinguishes these insurance institutions from the Imam Khomeini Relief Committee, an assistance provider, and from household cash subsidies known as yaraneh. [s3]

These distinctions prevent a misleading picture of a single welfare counter serving everyone on identical terms. Insurance, income-tested assistance and subsidy compensation have different institutional histories and eligibility principles. A household may also have links to more than one institution. [s3]

content.heading: What coverage figures can establish
content.content:
Research drawing on the Iran Social Survey, conducted in 2016, found that household connections to welfare institutions did not fit a simple division between poor assistance recipients and affluent insured workers. Social insurance also reached poorer households, while overlapping institutional connections were more common among better-off households. These are historical survey findings, not a current administrative count. [s3]

A recent UNICEF-hosted assessment likewise separates contributory social insurance from non-contributory assistance and describes a wider network of institutions providing social protection. This is a useful reading framework: first identify the benefit, then the institution, then the population entitled to receive it. Counting programmes or registrations alone cannot establish whether protection is adequate for a particular household. [s4]

name: Retirement
description: Retirement protection in Iran is organized through multiple contributory pension arrangements. Eligibility depends on the applicable fund and contribution history, while recent reforms have changed required contribution periods.

seo.title: Retirement in Iran: Pension Arrangements and Reform
seo.description: Explore Iran’s contributory pension arrangements, the role of contribution histories, and the limits of simplified retirement-age comparisons.

content.heading: Retirement is an insurance relationship
content.content:
Iran’s pension landscape consists of multiple arrangements rather than a single universal retirement payment. A World Bank study published in 2023 describes a system of contributory, defined-benefit pension funds. In a defined-benefit arrangement, pension entitlement follows a prescribed calculation rather than simply paying out an individual investment account. The study identifies informal and seasonal work as important locations of gaps in pension insurance. Its institutional counts and coverage estimates describe the period studied and should not be treated as a current census. [s1]

The historical Social Security Law illustrates why both earnings and contribution records matter. Its retirement provisions calculate pensions using covered earnings and years of contribution. This legal architecture helps explain the distinction between reaching an age and establishing a pension entitlement, but the archived translation cannot by itself establish a claimant’s current eligibility. [s2]

content.heading: Why a single retirement age is misleading
content.content:
A Persian reproduction of the implementing regulation for Article 29 of the Seventh Development Plan describes increases in required contribution periods that vary with a person’s existing contribution history. It also identifies limits on those increases and exceptions governed by separate rules, including hazardous occupations and certain disability-related categories. These provisions should not be reduced to a claim that every worker must retire at one newly increased age. [s3]

The reproduced regulation also distinguishes continued employment from retirement before completing the additional required contribution period, with proportional pension provisions for qualifying cases. Because an official consolidated text and subsequent implementing amendments were not verified here, this account explains the reform’s structure rather than providing an eligibility calculator. [s3]

content.heading: Income protection and financial sustainability
content.content:
The World Bank’s historical household analysis finds that pensions and cash assistance play different distributional roles. Better-off households relied proportionally more on pensions, while poorer households relied more on cash transfers. The report describes pension adjustment mechanisms as helping protect purchasing power during the period examined. That finding does not guarantee that every pension subsequently kept pace with each household’s living costs. [s1]

The same study identifies population ageing as a source of growing pressure on pay-as-you-go pension finance, where current resources support current beneficiaries. Retirement policy therefore concerns both income security and the capacity to sustain payments over time. A useful assessment must keep eligibility, benefit adequacy and financing distinct: changing one does not demonstrate that the other two have improved. [s1]

name: Social Support
description: Social support in Iran includes household cash transfers, targeted assistance and services for people facing deprivation. Its effectiveness depends on purchasing power, identification of need and access to complementary services.

seo.title: Social Support in Iran: Cash Assistance and Welfare Services
seo.description: Learn how household transfers, targeted welfare services and child-sensitive support fit together in Iran’s social assistance landscape.

content.heading: Beyond employment-related insurance
content.content:
Social support addresses needs that cannot be understood solely through a person’s employment insurance. In Iran, it includes broad household transfers alongside more targeted cash, in-kind assistance and social services. Research by the International Policy Centre for Inclusive Growth identifies the State Welfare Organization and the Imam Khomeini Relief Foundation as major assistance providers, with provincial and local structures involved in implementation. [s1]

The same research describes the expansion of household cash compensation during subsidy reform. Although targeting poorer households was an initial objective, administrative difficulties helped produce very broad coverage. This history explains why a payment associated with welfare is not necessarily evidence that its recipient has been assessed as poor. [s1]

content.heading: Payments and purchasing power
content.content:
The World Bank’s Iran Economic Monitor describes how inflation weakened the real value of regular cash transfers and how additional payments responded to subsidy changes and economic shocks. Its household-survey analysis distinguishes regular transfers from a separate category combining temporary payments, scholarships and charity. That mixed category cannot be read as the spending or reach of a single programme. [s2]

For the period 2020/21–2022/23, the report finds that poorer households relied more on cash transfers, whereas better-off households relied more on pensions. It attributes an important part of the later poverty reduction to expanded temporary transfers. These findings concern the reporting periods studied; they do not establish current payment amounts or prove that every eligible household received adequate support. [s2]

content.heading: Combining money with services
content.content:
Cash-plus approaches combine financial assistance with services intended to address barriers that money alone may not remove. A UNICEF-hosted evaluability assessment describes interventions involving education, health and nutrition support, counselling, parental employability and vocational skills. Its distinction between programme design and demonstrated results is essential: an evaluability assessment examines whether an intervention is sufficiently defined and measurable for evaluation; it is not proof that the intended long-term effects have occurred. [s3]

UNICEF’s Iran programme also emphasizes identifying vulnerable households, mapping the needs of children with disabilities and improving monitoring. Its account notes particular disadvantages faced by rural girls and identifies data, targeting and legislative weaknesses. National coverage totals therefore need to be read alongside evidence about who is missed and whether suitable services are actually accessible. [s4]

The practical question is broader than whether a household receives a transfer. Social support must also be assessed against the needs it seeks to address: food security, education, health, disability inclusion and protection from deprivation. UNICEF presents these as connected policy objectives, rather than interchangeable outcomes established by a payment record. [s4]
